entities.label: Ancient Rome
entities.summary: The city of Rome and the state it ruled, from its traditional founding in 753 BCE through the kings, the Republic and the first emperors to Trajan, about 100 CE.

entities.label: Rome
entities.summary: The city on the Tiber, founded according to tradition on 21 April 753 BCE, later the capital of the Roman Empire.

entities.label: Ostia
entities.summary: The port of Rome at the mouth of the Tiber, traditionally built by king Ancus Marcius.

entities.label: Pompeii
entities.summary: A town that became a Roman colony in 80 BCE and was buried by Vesuvius in 79 CE.

entities.label: Cannae
entities.summary: A place on the Italian east coast where Hannibal destroyed a Roman army in 216 BCE.

entities.label: Antium
entities.summary: A town near Rome, the birthplace of Caligula and of Nero.

entities.label: Narnia
entities.summary: A town in Italy, the birthplace of Nerva.

entities.label: Falacrinae
entities.summary: A village near Reate, the birthplace of Vespasian.

entities.label: Carthage
entities.summary: The Phoenician city in Africa, Rome’s great rival, sacked by Rome in 146 BCE and later refounded; ancient authors date its founding to 814/813 or 825 BCE.

entities.label: Zama
entities.summary: A place in Africa where Scipio defeated Hannibal in 202 BCE.

entities.label: Alexandria
entities.summary: The city founded by Alexander the Great in 330 BCE, capital of the Ptolemaic kingdom, captured by Octavian in 30 BCE.

entities.label: Actium
entities.summary: A promontory at the entrance of the Gulf of Ambracia, off which Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BCE.

entities.label: Philippi
entities.summary: A town in Macedonia, renamed by Philip II in 356 BCE, where Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius in October 42 BCE.

entities.label: Pharsalus
entities.summary: A town in Thessaly near which Caesar defeated Pompey in 48 BCE.

entities.label: Carrhae
entities.summary: Harran in Mesopotamia, where the Parthians defeated Crassus in 53 BCE.

entities.label: Jerusalem
entities.summary: The capital of Judaea and the sacred city of Judaism, taken by Titus in 70 CE.

entities.label: Antioch
entities.summary: A city in Syria where Germanicus died in 19 CE.

entities.label: Lugdunum
entities.summary: Modern Lyon, the birthplace of Claudius.

entities.label: The Roman monarchy
entities.summary: Rome under seven kings, according to tradition for 243 years from the founding to the expulsion of Tarquin the Proud; the kings and their years rest on later tradition.

entities.label: The Roman Republic
entities.summary: The Republic founded after the expulsion of the last king – traditionally in 509 BCE; one Livius page gives 510, and Livius itself argues for about 507–505 – and governed by annual magistrates and the Senate until Augustus.

entities.label: The Roman Empire
entities.summary: The rule of the emperors, which began when Octavian accepted the title Augustus in January 27 BCE; Rome was its capital.

entities.label: The Senate
entities.summary: The supreme deliberative body of Rome, named after senex, “old man”; according to tradition Romulus chose its first hundred members, and later it consisted of former magistrates and those chosen by the censors.

facts.text: Deliberation and advice on the affairs of the state

entities.label: King of Rome
entities.summary: The kingship of early Rome, held according to tradition by seven kings.

entities.label: Consul
entities.summary: One of the two annually elected chief magistrates of the Republic, with command of the army and the highest judicial power; they chaired the Senate. The office was opened to plebeians in the 360s BCE.

entities.label: Dictator
entities.summary: An emergency magistrate with extraordinary powers for at most six months, appointed by a consul; first appointed in the first decade of the fifth century BCE and last in the ordinary way in 202 BCE, later revived by Sulla and Caesar.

entities.label: Tribune of the plebs
entities.summary: The defender of the plebeians, with a veto over consuls, praetors and quaestors; first two, later ten. Livius dates the office to about 490 BCE (494 in the traditional chronology).

entities.label: Censor
entities.summary: A magistrate created about 440 BCE who held the census every five years, oversaw public morals and let state contracts.

entities.label: Praetor
entities.summary: A magistrate for the administration of justice, created in 367 or 366 BCE; a second praetor was added in 242 BCE.

entities.label: Emperor (princeps)
entities.summary: The position of the Roman emperor: Augustus called himself princeps, “first senator”; he held the governorships of all provinces with armies, and his combination of offices made him essentially a king.

entities.label: The age of the kings
entities.summary: From the traditional founding of Rome to the traditional end of the monarchy.

entities.label: The Republic
entities.summary: From the end of the monarchy to the settlement of Augustus in 27 BCE; the beginning is dated 509, 510 or about 507–505 BCE.

entities.label: The Julio-Claudians
entities.summary: The rule of the house of Augustus, from his sole rule in 31 BCE to the death of Nero in 68 CE.

entities.label: The year of the four emperors
entities.summary: The civil war after Nero’s death, when Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian were emperors in turn.

entities.label: The Flavians
entities.summary: The rule of Vespasian and his sons Titus and Domitian.

entities.label: Nerva and Trajan
entities.summary: From the accession of Nerva in 96 CE to the death of Trajan in 117 CE; this collection follows it to about 100 CE.

entities.label: The Julio-Claudians
entities.summary: The first imperial house, named after the Julian family of Augustus and the Claudian family of Tiberius; it ruled from 31 BCE to 68 CE.

entities.label: The Flavians
entities.summary: The house of Vespasian, emperor from 69 CE, and his sons Titus and Domitian; it ended with the murder of Domitian in 96 CE.

entities.label: Romulus
entities.summary: The legendary founder and first king of Rome, said to be a son of Rhea Silvia and the god Mars; there are no indications that he existed. Tradition gives him 37 years of rule.

facts.text: Legendary founder of Rome.

entities.label: Numa Pompilius
entities.summary: A Sabine, the second king of Rome according to tradition, who gave the Romans laws, customs and religious rites; tradition gives him 43 years.

facts.text: Laws and religious rites of Rome.

entities.label: Tullus Hostilius
entities.summary: The third king of Rome according to tradition, who conquered the Albans; tradition gives him 32 years.

facts.text: Conquest of the Albans.

entities.label: Ancus Marcius
entities.summary: The fourth king of Rome according to tradition, a grandson of Numa through a daughter, who founded Ostia; tradition gives him 24 years.

facts.text: Founded Ostia.

entities.label: Tarquinius Priscus
entities.summary: An Etruscan who became the fifth king of Rome according to tradition and began the Capitol; tradition gives him 38 years.

facts.text: Began the Capitol.

entities.label: Servius Tullius
entities.summary: The sixth king of Rome according to tradition, who held the first census; tradition gives him 45 years.

facts.text: The first census.

entities.label: Tarquinius Superbus
entities.summary: Tarquin the Proud, son of Tarquinius Priscus and son-in-law of Servius Tullius, the seventh and last king of Rome according to tradition, who was expelled; tradition gives him 25 years.

facts.text: The last king of Rome.

entities.label: Rhea Silvia
entities.summary: In the legend, the mother of Romulus; the father is said to be the god Mars.

facts.text: Mother of Romulus in the legend.

entities.label: The founding of Rome
entities.summary: According to tradition Romulus founded Rome on the Palatine on 21 April 753 BCE; Livius calls this Varronian date an artificial calculation.

entities.label: Lucius Junius Brutus
entities.summary: The legendary founder of the Republic, kin of the royal Tarquins, who according to tradition drove out the last king and was one of the first two consuls; he died in the first year of the Republic.

facts.text: Legendary founder of the Roman Republic.

entities.label: Marcus Furius Camillus
entities.summary: A Roman leader whom Livy’s summaries connect with the deliverance of Rome from the Gauls and with the time of the Licinian-Sextian laws.

facts.text: Leader in the years after the Gallic sack.

entities.label: The founding of the Republic
entities.summary: The last king was expelled and the Republic founded – in 509 BCE according to the traditional chronology, in 510 according to one Livius page, about 507–505 according to Livius’ own reconstruction.

entities.label: The Twelve Tables
entities.summary: The first codification of Roman law, written by a board of ten men in the middle of the fifth century BCE: ten tables in 451 and two more in 450 BCE in the traditional chronology.

entities.label: The Gauls take Rome
entities.summary: After their victory at the Allia the Gauls occupied Rome and besieged the Capitol until the Romans bought their freedom with gold – in 390 BCE in the traditional chronology, in 387 or 386 according to Livius.

entities.label: The Licinian-Sextian laws
entities.summary: Laws first proposed in 376 and passed in 367 BCE (traditional chronology) that opened the consulship to plebeians, adjusted debts and limited the ownership of public land.

entities.label: Hamilcar Barca
entities.summary: A Carthaginian general, the father of Hannibal.

facts.text: Father of Hannibal.

entities.label: Hannibal
entities.summary: The Carthaginian general, born at Carthage in 247 BCE, who crossed the Alps in the Second Punic War, destroyed a Roman army at Cannae and was defeated at Zama; he poisoned himself at Libyssa in the winter of 183/182 BCE.

facts.text: Crossed the Alps and won at Cannae.

entities.label: Scipio Africanus
entities.summary: Publius Cornelius Scipio, who took Cartagena, ended the war in Spain in 206 BCE and defeated Hannibal at Zama; he died at Liternum in 183 BCE.

facts.text: Defeated Hannibal at Zama.

entities.label: Cato the Elder
entities.summary: Marcus Porcius Cato, censor in 184 BCE, who argued for war against Carthage.

facts.text: Urged the destruction of Carthage.

entities.label: The First Punic War
entities.summary: The war of Rome and Carthage from 264 to 241 BCE, in which Rome conquered Sicily.

entities.label: The Second Punic War
entities.summary: The war of Rome and Carthage from 218 to 202 BCE, in which Hannibal crossed the Alps; the peace was signed in 201 BCE.

entities.label: The battle of Cannae
entities.summary: On 2 August 216 BCE Hannibal destroyed the army of the two Roman consuls at Cannae.

entities.label: The battle of Zama
entities.summary: On 19 October 202 BCE Scipio defeated Hannibal at Zama in Africa.

entities.label: The Third Punic War
entities.summary: The last war against Carthage, begun in 149 BCE after Cato had urged it; it ended in 146 BCE with the destruction of the city.

entities.label: The destruction of Carthage
entities.summary: In 146 BCE Rome took and sacked Carthage; Corinth was sacked in the same year.

entities.label: Tiberius Gracchus
entities.summary: A tribune of the plebs who in 133 BCE proposed a land bill limiting the holding of public land, and was killed on the Capitol in the same year.

facts.text: His land bill as tribune in 133 BCE.

entities.label: Gaius Gracchus
entities.summary: Brother of Tiberius, tribune in 123 and again in 122 BCE, who passed a grain law, a land bill and colonies, one of them at Carthage; he died in 121 BCE.

facts.text: His laws as tribune in 123 and 122 BCE.

entities.label: The tribunate of Tiberius Gracchus
entities.summary: In 133 BCE Tiberius Gracchus proposed his land bill; he was killed on the Capitol in the same year.

entities.label: Gaius Marius
entities.summary: Leader of the populares, consul seven times from 107 to 86 BCE, who reformed the army and defeated Jugurtha, the Teutones (102) and the Cimbri (101); married to Julia, an aunt of Julius Caesar, he died in 86 BCE.

facts.text: Seven consulships and the reform of the army.

entities.label: Sulla
entities.summary: A leader of the optimates who marched on Rome in 88 BCE, beginning the first civil war; after his return from Asia he became dictator and published lists of the proscribed. He died in 78 BCE.

facts.text: His march on Rome and his dictatorship.

entities.label: The Social War
entities.summary: The war with Rome’s Italian allies, which began in 91 BCE; citizenship was promised to loyal allies in 90 and to those who surrendered in 89. Marius and Sulla fought on the Roman side.

entities.label: Spartacus
entities.summary: The leader of a slave revolt that began at Capua and grew into a full-scale war in 73–71 BCE; his body was never found.

facts.text: Led the slave revolt of 73–71 BCE.

entities.label: Marcus Licinius Crassus
entities.summary: Born in 115 BCE and said to be the richest man in Rome, he suppressed the revolt of Spartacus as praetor in 71 BCE, joined Caesar and Pompey in 60 BCE and was killed after his defeat at Carrhae in 53 BCE.

facts.text: The richest man in Rome; defeated at Carrhae.

entities.label: The revolt of Spartacus
entities.summary: A slave revolt that began at Capua and was suppressed by Crassus; the Livius page dates the war 73–71 BCE in one place and 73–70 in another.

entities.label: Pompey
entities.summary: Gnaeus Pompeius, Pompey the Great, born in 106 BCE, who defeated the pirates and Mithridates and annexed Syria, married Caesar’s daughter Julia, was consul without a colleague in 52 BCE, and was murdered in Egypt in 48 BCE after Pharsalus.

facts.text: His victories in the east and his war with Caesar.

entities.label: Cicero
entities.summary: The orator, born in 106 BCE, who as consul discovered the conspiracy of Catilina; proscribed by the triumvirs, he was killed in 43 BCE.

facts.text: Orator; discovered the conspiracy of Catilina.

entities.label: Gaius Julius Caesar
entities.summary: Born on 13 July 100 BCE, consul in 59, conqueror of Gaul, who crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, defeated Pompey, became dictator for ten years in 46 and for life in 44, and was murdered on the Ides of March 44 BCE.

facts.text: Conquered Gaul and made himself dictator.

entities.label: Julia
entities.summary: Daughter of Julius Caesar by Cornelia, married to Pompey to seal the alliance of 60 BCE.

facts.text: Wife of Pompey, daughter of Caesar.

entities.label: The alliance of Caesar, Crassus and Pompey
entities.summary: In 60 BCE Caesar, Crassus and Pompey made a private agreement, sealed by Pompey’s marriage to Caesar’s daughter Julia; modern historians call it the First Triumvirate.

entities.label: Caesar conquers Gaul
entities.summary: From 58 to 50 BCE Caesar conquered Gaul; in 52 BCE Vercingetorix surrendered to him at Alesia.

entities.label: The battle of Carrhae
entities.summary: In 53 BCE the Parthians defeated the Roman army of Crassus at Carrhae; Crassus was killed.

entities.label: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
entities.summary: In the night of 10/11 January 49 BCE Caesar crossed the Rubicon, the border of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy, and began the second civil war; where the river was is not certain.

entities.label: The battle of Pharsalus
entities.summary: On 9 August 48 BCE Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus; Pompey fled to Egypt and was murdered there.

entities.label: Marcus Junius Brutus
entities.summary: Born about 85 BCE, son of Servilia, one of the murderers of Caesar and one of the last defenders of the Republic; he took his own life after Philippi in 42 BCE.

facts.text: One of the murderers of Caesar.

entities.label: The murder of Caesar
entities.summary: On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, Caesar was murdered by a group led by Gaius Cassius, Decimus Brutus and Marcus Junius Brutus.

entities.label: Mark Antony
entities.summary: Born in 83 BCE (82 according to another Livius page), a member of the Second Triumvirate, partner of Cleopatra, defeated at Actium; he took his own life on 12 August 30 BCE.

facts.text: Triumvir; defeated at Actium.

entities.label: Cleopatra VII
entities.summary: Queen of Egypt from 51 to 30 BCE, born in December 70 or January 69 BCE; partner of Julius Caesar and then of Mark Antony, she died on 12 August 30 BCE, reportedly by suicide.

facts.text: Last queen of Ptolemaic Egypt.

entities.label: The Second Triumvirate
entities.summary: In 43 BCE Antony and Octavian became triumvirs with a third colleague, an official magistracy with dictatorial powers.

entities.label: The battle of Philippi
entities.summary: In October 42 BCE Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius at Philippi.

entities.label: The battle of Actium
entities.summary: Octavian, with Agrippa, defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra off Actium in 31 BCE – on 2 September according to the battle page, on 2 August according to another Livius page.

entities.label: The settlement of Augustus
entities.summary: In January 27 BCE Octavian accepted the title Augustus (16 January); the rule of the emperors begins here.

entities.label: Augustus
entities.summary: Born Gaius Octavius in Rome on 23 September 63 BCE, son of Gaius Octavius and Atia and adopted by his great-uncle Julius Caesar in 44 BCE; sole ruler from 31 BCE and the first emperor from 27 BCE until his death on 19 August 14 CE. Modern writers call him Octavian before 27 BCE, a name he never used.

facts.text: The first Roman emperor.

entities.label: Livia
entities.summary: Born in January 58 BCE, wife first of Tiberius Claudius Nero, by whom she was the mother of Tiberius, and from 17 January 38 BCE of Octavian; she died in 29 CE.

facts.text: Wife of Augustus, mother of Tiberius.

entities.label: Tiberius
entities.summary: Born in Rome in 42 BCE, son of Livia and stepson of Augustus, who adopted him on 26 June 4 CE; emperor from 14 to 37 CE, he died on 16 March 37 CE.

facts.text: Second Roman emperor.

entities.label: Germanicus
entities.summary: Born on 24 May 15 BCE, son of Drusus and Antonia, adopted by Tiberius and married to Agrippina the Elder; father of Caligula and Agrippina the Younger, he died at Antioch on 10 October 19 CE.

facts.text: Father of Caligula.

entities.label: Caligula
entities.summary: Son of Germanicus, born at Antium on 31 August 12 CE; emperor from 37 to 41 CE, he was murdered by Cassius Chaerea on 24 January 41 CE.

facts.text: Murdered after four years as emperor.

entities.label: Claudius
entities.summary: Son of Drusus and Antonia, born at Lugdunum on 1 August 10 BCE; emperor from 41 to 54 CE, he married Agrippina the Younger, adopted her son Nero in 50 CE and died, poisoned, on 13 October 54 CE.

facts.text: Emperor who adopted Nero.

entities.label: Agrippina the Younger
entities.summary: Daughter of Germanicus, born at Cologne in 15 or 16 CE, wife of Claudius (married in 48 or 49 CE) and mother of Nero; she was killed in March 59 CE.

facts.text: Wife of Claudius, mother of Nero.

entities.label: Nero
entities.summary: Son of Agrippina the Younger, born at Antium on 15 December 37 CE and adopted by Claudius in 50 CE; emperor from 54 to 68 CE, his reign ended with the revolts of Vindex, Macer and Galba and his suicide in June 68 CE.

facts.text: The last Julio-Claudian emperor.

entities.label: Galba
entities.summary: Born near Tarracina on 24 December 3 BCE, he revolted in Spain in April 68 and was emperor from June 68; he was lynched in Rome in January 69 CE (one Livius page says 15 June 69).

facts.text: First emperor of the year of the four emperors.

entities.label: Otho
entities.summary: Born on 28 April 32 CE, he came to power in 69 CE by bribing the praetorian guard and took his own life on 16 April 69 after his army was defeated by that of Vitellius.

facts.text: Emperor for three months in 69 CE.

entities.label: Vitellius
entities.summary: Born on 7 September 15 CE, proclaimed emperor by his troops on 2 January 69 and recognised by the Senate after Otho’s death; he was killed on 20 December 69 CE when Rome was taken by the army of Vespasian.

facts.text: Emperor in 69 CE.

entities.label: Vespasian
entities.summary: Born at Falacrinae on 17 November 9 CE, sent by Nero to suppress the Jewish revolt, proclaimed emperor in Alexandria on 1 July 69; emperor until his death on 23 June 79 CE, he built the Colosseum.

facts.text: Founder of the Flavian house.

entities.label: Titus
entities.summary: Son of Vespasian, born in Rome on 30 December 39 CE, who took Jerusalem in 70 CE; emperor from 79 to 81, in whose reign Vesuvius erupted and the Colosseum was dedicated. He died on 13 September 81 CE.

facts.text: Took Jerusalem in 70 CE.

entities.label: Domitian
entities.summary: Son of Vespasian, born in Rome on 24 October 51 CE, emperor from 81 to 96 CE; he was murdered by courtiers on 18 September 96 CE.

facts.text: The last Flavian emperor.

entities.label: Nerva
entities.summary: Born at Narnia on 30 November 30 CE, emperor from 18 September 96 CE, who adopted Trajan in 97; he died in January 98 CE.

facts.text: Adopted Trajan as his successor.

entities.label: Trajan
entities.summary: Born at Italica on 18 September 53 CE, adopted by Nerva in 97 and emperor from 28 January 98 CE until his death on 7 August 117; he conquered Dacia and made Arabia Petraea a province in 106.

facts.text: Conquered Dacia.

entities.label: The battle in the Teutoburg Forest
entities.summary: In September 9 CE Arminius, leading a coalition of Germanic tribes, annihilated three Roman legions under Publius Quintilius Varus; Germania remained independent.

entities.label: The death of Augustus
entities.summary: Augustus died on 19 August 14 CE and Tiberius succeeded him.

entities.label: The Great Fire of Rome
entities.summary: The great fire of Rome in 64 CE, under Nero.

entities.label: The death of Nero
entities.summary: After the revolts of Vindex, Macer and Galba Nero took his own life in June 68 CE – on 9 June according to his page, on 8 June according to the chronology of 68–70.

entities.label: The year of the four emperors
entities.summary: In 69 CE Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian were emperors in turn; Vespasian was recognised on 21 December 69.

entities.label: The Jewish War
entities.summary: The war in Judaea that began in 66 CE and culminated in the destruction of the temple of Jerusalem in 70; the last resistance at Masada held out until 74.

entities.label: The siege of Jerusalem
entities.summary: Titus began the siege of Jerusalem on 14 April 70 CE and was master of the city on 8 September.

entities.label: The eruption of Vesuvius
entities.summary: In 79 CE, in the reign of Titus, Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii.

entities.label: The dedication of the Colosseum
entities.summary: The Amphitheatrum Flavium, built by Vespasian, was dedicated by Titus in 80 CE.

entities.label: The murder of Domitian
entities.summary: Domitian was murdered by courtiers on 18 September 96 CE; Nerva became emperor the same day.

entities.label: Trajan becomes emperor
entities.summary: On Nerva’s death in January 98 CE Trajan, his adopted son, became emperor.

relations.label: Held the office of
relations.note: One of the first two consuls, according to tradition.

relations.label: Held the office of
relations.note: For ten years and then for life.
